abstract: Diagnosing failures in LLM agents remains largely manual. Practitioners inspect a small subset of execution traces, form ad-hoc hypotheses, and iterate. This process misses patterns that only emerge across trace populations and does not scale to production corpora where individual traces span tens of thousands of tokens. We formalize the problem of corpus-level trace diagnostics. Given a corpus of execution traces, the goal is to produce grounded natural-language insights that characterize systematic behavioral patterns across trace groups, each linked to supporting evidence. We present the Insights Generator (IG), a multi-agent system that answers diagnostic questions by proposing and testing hypotheses across the trace corpus to produce an evidence-backed insights report. We evaluate IG across qualitative and objective dimensions, spanning rubric-based report assessment and downstream performance improvements achieved by implementing IG insights. Human experts using IG reports improve scaffold performance by 30.4 pp over the unmodified baseline scaffold, and coding agents leveraging IG-derived insights show consistent and stable gains. Across benchmarks, IG's scout-investigator architecture produces findings comparable in detection coverage to competing approaches, while domain experts rated IG reports as leading depth and evidence quality.

title: Behavioral Integrity Verification for AI Agent Skills
ss_tldr: Behavioral integrity auditing for agent skills at scale is demonstrated by the BIV framework, which outperforms state-of-the-art rule-based and single-pass LLM baselines on a 906-skill malicious-skill detection benchmark.
abstract: Agent skills extend LLM agents with privileged third-party capabilities such as filesystem access, credentials, network calls, and shell execution. Existing safety work catches malicious prompts and risky runtime actions, but the skill artifact itself goes unverified. We formalize this as the behavioral integrity verification (BIV) problem: a typed set comparison between declared and actual capabilities over a shared taxonomy that bridges code, instructions, and metadata. The BIV framework instantiates this comparison by pairing deterministic code analysis with LLM-assisted capability extraction. The resulting structured evidence supports three downstream analyses: deviation taxonomy, root-cause classification, and malicious-skill detection. On 49,943 skills from the OpenClaw registry, the deviation taxonomy reveals a pervasive description-implementation gap: 80.0% of skills have at least one deviation in the taxonomy, with four compound-threat categories surfaced. Root-cause classification finds that deviations are mostly oversight, not malice: 81.1% trace to developer oversight and 18.9% to adversarial intent, with 5.0% of skills carrying predicted multi-stage attack chains. On a 906-skill malicious-skill detection benchmark, BIV reaches an F1 of 0.949, outperforming state-of-the-art rule-based and single-pass LLM baselines. These results demonstrate behavioral integrity auditing for agent skills at scale.

title: Homeostatic Continual Learning
ss_tldr: A method that enables an AI agent to learn continuously in a changing environment without catastrophic forgetting is proposed and the works needed to render the method practical, the connections to many fields in Artificial Intelligence and the broader implications of the method are discussed.
abstract: I formulate a Continual Learning problem for an autonomous agent that imitates the one animals face. The agent has intents to satisfy. It experiences contexts where different combinations of features are active and impact intent outcomes. I propose a method named ``Homeostatic Continual Learning'' that imitates the one animals use. The agent learns incrementally environment data and features relevant for their intents from the impact of contexts, gradually completes its model and policy and performs well in more and more contexts. The core of the method is to find outliers in the environment data when the agent experiences an outlier in its intent outcome after the context changes. This method enables the agent to learn continuously in changing contexts without catastrophic forgetting. When pursuing many intents concurrently, the agent may build a transformer-like world model with the method where it factorizes the objects in the world into features, abstract objects into comparable instances of concepts and map concepts to intents through features. The world model is composed of semantic nodes and explainable by nature. I discuss the works needed to render the method practical, the connections to many fields in Artificial Intelligence and the broader implications of the method.

title: Balance of Benchmarks: Evidence Retention and Multiplicity-Aware Model Comparison
ss_tldr: Balance of Benchmarks is introduced, a framework that retains eligible benchmark evidence while adapting its influence for task-conditioned model comparison using only public aggregate scores, and makes benchmark inclusion, redundancy, and task relevance explicit and testable measurement choices.
abstract: Benchmark aggregation requires decisions about how much evidence to use and how much influence each benchmark receives. Curated suites control influence through selection, which can exclude informative observations. A broader pool can retain those observations. With equal weighting, repeated or closely related benchmarks gain influence as their number grows. We introduce Balance of Benchmarks (BoB) to retain eligible observations and control their influence separately. We fit benchmark-specific response curves to place different difficulty ranges on a shared ability scale and use description similarity to downweight benchmarks in crowded neighborhoods. We test retention and density weighting in separate interventions on WildScores, a sparse collection of 148 developer-reported benchmarks, using 14 Artificial Analysis benchmarks as a controlled reference. With the model population fixed and entire source-lineage families held out, suite expansion improves held-out prediction under BoB and equal-weight equating on both WildScores and BIG-bench. Under substantial reporting overlap, density weighting improves robustness to multiplicity. Complete re-listings yield smaller mean rank displacement under BoB (0.63 versus 1.95 for equal-weight equating), with benefits also in paraphrased re-listings and supported affine fits. The benefit can reverse if models report different benchmarks, because a single weight per column gives models that report only part of a group less than its intended share. We therefore compute each model's weights from the benchmarks it reports. This rule removes the reversal in controlled re-listings and keeps held-out prediction close to that of equal weighting. These comparisons separate evidence retention, benchmark influence, and reporting coverage and show why repeated entries need to be handled per model.

title: The Missing Complement: State-Conditioned Minimal Sufficient Evidence for Coding Agents
ss_tldr: This work formulate state-conditioned minimal sufficient evidence recovery: given a captured agent state, recover a compact evidence combination supplying what its next decision still lacks supplying what its next decision still lacks.
abstract: Retrieval assembles repository context by ranking passages for relevance to the current query. A coding agent halfway through an issue has already read much of what such a ranker returns. Relevance is scored per passage, but sufficiency belongs to the set: independently scored passages can fill the budget with support for one requirement while another goes unmet. We formulate state-conditioned minimal sufficient evidence recovery: given a captured agent state, recover a compact evidence combination supplying what its next decision still lacks. SERBench measures this on 500 held-out states from 45 repositories, recording what the agent has seen, crediting only sets that satisfy every annotated evidence requirement of the current decision, and separating set recovery from candidate discovery. MSS-Complement treats acquisition as set construction, not ranking. Three semantic calls propose a jointly sufficient set, search for what it lacks, and return 4-8 intact source units within 6,144 tokens. One configuration, fixed on calibration data, recovers a complete set for 73.0% of those states at five items and 80.6% at eight, against 61.4% and 72.4% for Qwen3 embedding with reranking. A matched control ranking by similarity alone recovers fewer complete sets, placing the margin over it in the set-level policy, not the computation. The lead persists from frozen repository source with no gold-derived pool. On AMA-Bench it answers from a 76.2% smaller answer prompt, with accuracy 2.08 points above that benchmark's own memory agent. Removing one required group from a complete set costs repair-localization precision under two executors. Retrieval for agents is better posed as recovering what a decision lacks than re-ranking what an issue resembles.

title: QVAC Genesis III: A Large-Scale, High-Quality Open Synthetic STEM Corpus for Efficient Language Model Pre-Training
ss_tldr: This work introduces QVAC Genesis III, a 191.43B-token, STEM-focused multi-domain synthetic corpus covering 19 domains across several difficulty levels and different educational styles, and introduces an LLM-as-a-parser evaluation protocol that extracts final answers from free-form outputs and tracks both accuracy and answer validity.
abstract: High-quality pre-training data is a critical bottleneck for educational and STEM-specific language models targeting edge AI and on-device deployment where token budgets are tightly constrained. While major organizations train ever-larger models on private corpora, the open ecosystem lacks STEM-focused synthetic datasets that deliver high per-token learning value efficiently for small models. To address this gap, we introduce QVAC Genesis III, a 191.43B-token, STEM-focused multi-domain synthetic corpus covering 19 domains across several difficulty levels and different educational styles. QVAC Genesis III is built via a dual generation strategy that performs targeted teacher distillation using a weak edge-scale student model as signal: the student's failures are converted into corrective explanations, while its successes are expanded into contrastive option-level reasoning over all answer choices. We further introduce an LLM-as-a-parser evaluation protocol that extracts final answers from free-form outputs and tracks both accuracy and answer validity. To validate the effectiveness of our QVAC Genesis III data, we conduct controlled from-scratch ablations with 1.7B-parameter models, showing that models trained with QVAC Genesis III consistently outperform both models trained with the open-source synthetic corpus Cosmopedia-v2 and the publicly released Cosmo-1B model across ARC, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU STEM benchmarks, achieving up to +28.57% on ARC-E and +21.35% on ARC-C, while reaching a Valid Answer Rate of up to 99.45%.

title: CHORUS: Coverage-Guided Agentic RL and Policy Consolidation for Testbench Stimulus Generation
ss_tldr: CHORUS is presented, a post-training framework that pushes performance beyond what a conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT)-to-reinforcement learning (RL) pipeline achieves, and consolidates the resulting specialists into a single 4B model.
abstract: Testbenches written by large language models can compile and run while leaving entire datapaths idle. We present CHORUS, the first framework to combine coverage-guided agentic reinforcement learning (RL) with policy consolidation for testbench stimulus generation. We train LLM4Cov's final supervised checkpoint to draft testbenches and repair its lowest-scoring draft using simulator feedback, raising CVDP-ECov agentic Pass@1 from 69.2% to 85.5%. Applying the same training to three checkpoints yields similar overall pass rates, yet the policies succeed on different designs. Averaging their weights combines these strengths in a single dense 4B model that reaches 86.7% agentic Pass@1. When simulator rewards select the teacher for each training prompt, the distilled 4B model reaches 88.0%, 13.5 percentage points above DeepSeek-R1 (671B).

title: Cautious Context Steering for Language Model Personalization
ss_tldr: Cautious Context Steering (CCS), which adds a lightweight adapter to a frozen backbone LM to decide at each token whether and how strongly user context should affect generation, demonstrating robust generalization to new users and domains.
abstract: User context can personalize a language model without per-user fine-tuning, but its influence is not equally helpful at every token. Context Steering (CoS) uses a fixed steering strength throughout generation and requires two LM forward passes per step. We propose Cautious Context Steering (CCS), a lightweight adapter that learns when and how strongly to steer a frozen LM using user context. We train the adapter through cautious distillation, using oracle targets built from predictions with and without context. It learns to match the steered distribution where context helps predict the user's preferred token and the context-free base distribution elsewhere. The CCS adapter outperforms both training-free context-based methods and trained personalization baselines in preference alignment across benchmarks. We also introduce GSM8K-P to evaluate task accuracy and task-specific format preferences together. CCS achieves high format adherence while maintaining task accuracy, offering a better balance than the baselines. The CCS adapter adds less than 0.4% of the backbone's parameters. At inference, each decoding step uses one context-conditioned LM forward pass and a lightweight adapter evaluation, reducing generation time on PRISM by approximately 35-36% compared with CoS.

title: Relax Within, Balance Across: Load Balancing under Composition Shifts in Vision-Language Mixture-of-Experts
ss_tldr: Across four split backbones, ReBA lowers load on every reported benchmark input while keeping mean task accuracy comparable to Std-Aux, and lowers average load over the tested range and worst physical load under resolution and tiling shifts.
abstract: Vision-language mixture-of-experts (MoE) models such as Qwen3-VL need balanced loads for fast parallel serving. Standard training pools image and text tokens into one auxiliary loss, assuming training balance holds at inference. Yet we find a surprising mismatch: on a fixed router, balance shifts sharply whenever resolution, dynamic tiling, or image count changes the image-to-text token ratio. Splitting load by modality reveals cross-modal load cancellation: opposing image and text errors cancel near the training ratio, hiding strong skew until the mix changes. To quantify this shift, we derive an exact quadratic law: under fixed modality profiles, one reference run predicts the full response curve, and the image-text gap governs sensitivity. Meanwhile, patches within an image route similarly while patch counts vary, letting large images dominate flat pooling. We propose ReBA (Relax Within, Balance Across) to separate modality losses by token fraction and weight images equally, letting each image specialize while keeping overall visual load even. Across four split backbones, ReBA turns fragile single-ratio balance into stable balance across resolutions, tilings, and image counts without hurting accuracy. Large modality gaps in released native MoEs also show its promise for native post-training. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiangWu-77/ReBA.

title: Accounting for Purchased Artificial Intelligence Inference in Corporate Greenhouse Gas Inventories: A Token-Based Method
ss_tldr: This paper sets out a token-based method and open dataset: a cradle-to-gate boundary, four tiers of activity data, an effective-token basis, a four-term factor (serving electricity, embodied hardware, data-centre construction, disclosed final training runs) and a rule resolving any model identifier and region to a factor.
abstract: Purchased artificial intelligence (AI) inference belongs in Scope 3 Category 1 of a corporate greenhouse gas inventory, yet practice omits it or applies a spend-based factor that gives 1.7 to 12.3 times the physical estimate and cannot tell one model or region from another. This paper sets out a token-based method and open dataset: a cradle-to-gate boundary, four tiers of activity data, an effective-token basis, a four-term factor (serving electricity, embodied hardware, data-centre construction, disclosed final training runs) and a rule resolving any model identifier and region to a factor. Inference footprints span twelve times between model classes and nine between regions. The mid-class factor, 0.039 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per million billed tokens at the world-average grid, is the low end of a stated structural range: a less efficient serving configuration raises it 2.8 times, and replacing the training term with all model development, on its own boundary, gives 1.5 to 2.9 times it. Input bands alone give -18% to +29%. Published per-query energy estimates that can describe a mid-class model are 2.4 to 7.2 times the mid-class energy, above its structural range in four of five rows; those that can describe a frontier-class model bracket it at 0.7 to 1.6 times. Worked examples give 8.5 kg CO2e a year for a 200-person firm, and 2.1 tonnes for fifty developers using agentic coding tools on a mid-class model or 8.3 tonnes on a frontier-class one. The contribution is a traceable figure; accuracy against metered energy is untested.

title: Periodic and Harmonic Periodic RoPE for Length Extrapolation in LLMs
ss_tldr: This work proposes Periodic RoPE (P-RoPE), a positional encoding mechanism designed to circumvent position exhaustion that outperforms MiniMInd with standard GPT architectures in long-context efficiency and stability and provides a possible pathway toward LLMs with genuine infinite-context understanding.
abstract: The ability to process long contexts is crucial for large language models (LLMs) to perform long-horizon tasks. Rotary position embedding (RoPE) gives every token a new rotation angle, so a model eventually meets angles it never saw in training, i.e., position exhaustion. We propose Periodic RoPE (P-RoPE), a positional encoding mechanism that operates in conjunction with sliding window attention. It repeats the first sliding-window-size \(W\) angles of the RoPE table, so the model needs only \(W\) distinct angles. P-RoPE works but introduces a wrap error at the window boundary. We further propose Harmonic Periodic RoPE (HP-RoPE), which removes the error by choosing frequencies that complete whole turns in \(W\) tokens. We compare models that share the same architecture, data, and schedule and differ only in the window-layer position encoding: standard RoPE, P-RoPE, and HP-RoPE. The results show that P-RoPE and HP-RoPE keep perplexity nearly flat from the training length \(768\) to \(16\)k, while RoPE, NTK, and YaRN rise. In a format-free Passkey test at \(16\)k, they remain at \(99\)--\(100\%\), against \(11\)--\(37\%\) for those RoPE interpolations. The code is available at \href{https://github.com/Cominder/miniwin}{https://github.com/Cominder/miniwin}.

title: VESTA: Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents
ss_tldr: It is found that VESTA's dynamic tool creation outperforms prior agentic pipelines, with the largest gains on complex and domain-specific tasks.
abstract: Fitting quantitative models to data is a central step in scientific workflows, yet it remains one of the least automated. Recent agent-based systems leverage language and vision-language models (VLMs) to propose statistical models, but these systems struggle on challenging modeling tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce VESTA (Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents), a framework that equips VLMs with a dynamically growing toolkit to guide model refinement through data transformations, hypothesis-driven visualizations, and statistical tests. Unlike prior systems that rely on iterative critique alone, VESTA explores data before and during refinement by selecting or creating reusable diagnostic tools. We evaluate VESTA using three toolkit configurations: no tools, static expert-written tools, and dynamic model-written tools. To support this evaluation, we introduce DAWN (Dataset for Automated Workflows and Numerical Modeling), a benchmark targeting distribution fitting and time series modeling with varying difficulty tiers that culminates in real-world astronomy tasks including modeling initial mass functions and gravitational-wave chirp signals. VESTA's dynamic tool creation outperforms prior agentic pipelines for statistical analysis and visual tool creation, with the largest gains on complex and domain-specific tasks. Against strong agentic coding harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode), VESTA is better on all time series tasks and on complex distribution fitting tasks, though the harnesses achieve better fits on simpler distributions. Further, dynamically generated tools are substantially more sophisticated than those produced by existing visual tool-creation systems, covering more diagnostic categories per function and strongly preferring visual outputs that the VESTA VLM critic can reason over directly.

title: From Portraits to Pathology: Probing Diagnostic Overreach in Vision-Language Models
ss_tldr: It is shown that most baseline open-model refusals fail to explain both the insufficiency of facial evidence and the need for clinical assessment, underscoring the need for stronger safety measures in model training and deployment.
abstract: Many medical conditions require clinical assessment of symptoms, history, and functioning rather than judgments from appearance. We study whether vision-language models (VLMs) abstain from facial attribution of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), major depressive disorder (MDD), and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).   To support this study, we construct PARITY (Paired Assessment with Reused Identity), a demographically balanced dataset for testing whether changing facial expressions alters diagnostic judgments, while holding identity and other visual factors as constant as possible.   Our comprehensive evaluation of 27 open- and closed-weight models reveals inconsistent abstention across expressions, conditions, and task formats. Models turn facial expressions into unsupported medical judgments: this behavior is widespread among open-weight VLMs and extends to safety-trained frontier models that abstain on individual portraits yet make diagnostic judgments when comparing portraits of the same identity. Safeguard checks reveal further gaps: clinical instructions do not consistently prevent these judgments, and a guardrail model rarely flags paired requests as unsafe. Semantic analysis further shows that most baseline open-model refusals fail to explain both the insufficiency of facial evidence and the need for clinical assessment. Unsupported judgments and seemingly authoritative explanations can cause distress, reinforce stigma, and offer false reassurance, underscoring the need for stronger safety measures in model training and deployment.

title: AI Tour Meeting: Group Travel Planning by LLM Agents
ss_tldr: The utility of the framework is demonstrated by presenting system validation and several analytical results obtained by the framework by presenting system validation and several analytical results obtained by the framework.
abstract: This paper proposes AI Tour Meeting, a group travel planning framework powered by multiple Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents. The agents are instantiated with distinct personas and collaboratively seek an itinerary that satisfies their constraints and preferences through natural language discussion. The framework enables easy and flexible orchestration of such discussions by providing interfaces for configuring agent personas, discussion workflows, monitoring, and LLM deployment. Its primary use case is a simulation tool for analyzing the behavior of multiple LLM agents during tour planning discussions. This paper demonstrates the utility of the framework by presenting system validation and several analytical results obtained by the framework.

title: When Does Depth Matter For In-Context Learning? Adaptive Inference in Deep Transformers
ss_tldr: The results suggest that depth and feedforward blocks enable transformers to implement adaptive inference, and this is advantageous when the distribution over latent variables has hierarchical structure.
abstract: Transformers perform computations through many successive attention and feedforward blocks, allowing them to learn complex correlations between a large collection of coupled variables. When does stacking successive attention-feedforward computations over many layers provide a computational advantage over a single transformer block? We address this question by examining in-context learning in generalized linear attention transformers. We first introduce a general theory of distributed inference in such transformers, subject to constraints on communication and depth. We show that such systems can exploit internal representations (`function vectors') to infer a latent context variable at increasingly finer scales over its layers. For an in-context linear regression task, the theory predicts that while one-layer transformers without feedforward blocks are optimal for Gaussian priors over the context variable, multi-layer transformers are superior for non-Gaussian, tree-like priors. Trained linear attention transformers reproduce quantitative predictions from the theory. Using causal key-patching experiments, we verify that function vectors in intermediate layers mediate adaptive routing of information. Our results suggest that depth and feedforward blocks enable transformers to implement adaptive inference, and this is advantageous when the distribution over latent variables has hierarchical structure.

title: Spectral Vision Transformer for Efficient Tokenization with Limited Data
abstract: Vision transformers tokenize an image into patches, which couples the token count to resolution and requires the embedding to be learned from data. We propose a spectral vision transformer architecture for efficient tokenization in the limited-data regime, with an emphasis on medical imaging. Rather than using spatial patches, we tokenize into coefficients of a fixed basis. This approach defines each token as one spectral mode, and the sequence length is chosen rather than implied by resolution, reducing the cost of attention. Our proposed spectral ViT shows superior or comparable performance where data is scarce in public medical imaging benchmarks, natural images, object shapes, simulations, and protected clinical data. We release our code at: https://github.com/agr78/SpectralViT.

title: LimiX-2: A Contextual Mechanism Network Towards General Structured-Data Intelligence
abstract: We introduce LimiX-2, a new model in the LimiX family, developed through model and data scaling guided by our previously established scaling laws. LimiX-2 adopts the Contextual Mechanism Networks (CMNs) paradigm and is pretrained with Context-Conditional Masked Modeling (CCMM). CMNs shifts the organizing principle of in-context learning from target-centric prediction to mechanism-oriented joint modeling. Rather than centering the network on the $p(y \mid x, D_{\mathrm{context}})$ objective of conventional tabular PFNs, it is designed around learning $p(x, y \mid D_{\mathrm{context}})$, a context-dependent representation of the joint structure underlying data generation. Pretraining uses synthetic datasets generated by structural causal models (SCMs) spanning diverse graph structures, functional mechanisms, and observation processes. Evaluations on TabArena, TALENT, and BCCO show that LimiX-2 outperforms current dataset-specific models and tabular foundation models. Beyond predictive performance, the CMN paradigm also promotes causal awareness in LimiX-2: its feature attention encodes direct causal relationships, enabling accurate causal skeleton recovery.

title: Measurement-Budget Allocation in Quantum Learning with Finite-Shot Generalization Guarantees
abstract: On near-term quantum hardware, estimating a Born probability requires repeated circuit executions. A quantum learning experiment with a fixed measurement budget $B$ must therefore decide how many distinct training states $n$ to use and how many shots $S$ to spend on each. We study this trade-off for binary quantum classifiers whose measurement operator $M$ is learned from the training data and evaluated with fresh measurement outcomes. We prove a distribution-free generalization bound for bounded, $L$-Lipschitz losses with a sample term of order $\sqrt{d/n}$ and a shot term of order $\sqrt{(\log n)/S}$; under $B=nS$ the two terms move in opposite directions. Minimizing a closed-form surrogate of the bound gives the allocation rule $n^* = 2\sqrt{2dB/\log(4B/δ)}$, $S^* = B/n^*$, whose bound value is within 0.1% of the exact numerical minimum on all budgets we evaluate, and a worst-case rate of $B^{-1/4}$. PennyLane simulations with 2- and 4-qubit variational circuits on nine synthetic benchmarks show that the empirical gap stays below the bound in all configurations, although the bound is vacuous at the simulated budgets and becomes non-vacuous only for larger budgets (e.g., $B \gtrsim 5000$ for $d=4$). For a loss that is concave in the score, the empirical gap is U-shaped under a fixed budget and the measured shot contribution matches its analytical value; for the absolute loss, shot noise is unbiased and no shot-limited regime appears. The rule can be used to plan finite-shot evaluations before an experiment is run.

title: From "Weak" Signals to Strong Models: Preference Delta Aggregation with LoRA Merging
ss_tldr: This work proposes Preference Delta Aggregation (PDA), the first framework that derives a preference delta from each weak-weaker model pair, instantiates it as a LoRA adapter learned through preference optimization, and aggregates the resulting deltas via LoRA merging.
abstract: Training strong large language models (LLMs) requires high-quality supervision, which is often scarce. Recent work shows that paired preference data from weak-weaker model pairs (e.g., Qwen3 4B over 1.7B), despite the limited quality of individual responses, can provide an effective supervision signal through relative quality deltas, which we term a "weak" signal. This motivates a key research question: can multiple "weak" signals be constructively aggregated for improving strong models (e.g., Qwen3 8B)? To this end, we propose Preference Delta Aggregation (PDA), the first framework that derives a preference delta from each weak-weaker model pair, instantiates it as a LoRA adapter learned through preference optimization, and aggregates the resulting deltas via LoRA merging. To improve the composition of independently trained adapters, we introduce Geometric Alignment Merging (GAM), which aligns their left and right singular bases through orthogonal Procrustes rotations and averages the aligned factors. Evaluations on knowledge reasoning and agentic search show that PDA-GAM exceeds the strongest individual delta, with further gains along the evaluated sequences of additional deltas. Using three reasoning deltas and four agentic deltas, PDA-GAM improves Qwen3-8B by 6.8 and 7.3 points on average, respectively, exceeding the strongest single-delta baseline by 2.1 and 4.3 points. These configurations achieve the highest average scores among the evaluated merging methods, with similar gains observed on a second student model. Further analysis suggests that these gains come from composing complementary capabilities encoded across distinct preference deltas. Code is available at https://github.com/AlbertQiSun/Preference-Delta-Aggregation.

title: SPARK: Adaptive Parametric Knowledge Participation for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
ss_tldr: SPARK is introduced, a novel framework that formulates parametric knowledge control as a latent participation policy learning problem, enabling LLMs to adaptively regulate the contribution of parametric knowledge during generation.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances the faithfulness of large language models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge into the generation process. However, conflicts between retrieved context and parametric knowledge can cause LLMs to rely on inconsistent internal knowledge, hindering their ability to faithfully leverage retrieved evidence. Existing approaches mitigate this issue by editing parametric knowledge to resolve such conflicts. However, locating and modifying knowledge encoded in model parameters is challenging and may inadvertently compromise the backbone LLM's capabilities. In this paper, we introduce SPARK, a novel framework that formulates parametric knowledge control as a latent participation policy learning problem, enabling LLMs to adaptively regulate the contribution of parametric knowledge during generation. Specifically, SPARK introduces a lightweight participation policy that dynamically modulates the contribution of FFN-mediated parametric knowledge while keeping the backbone LLM frozen. The participation policy is optimized with a faithfulness-oriented reward, enabling fine-grained control over parametric knowledge participation during generation. Extensive experiments on six datasets validate the effectiveness of SPARK, which introduces and optimizes only 0.01\% additional trainable parameters while keeping the backbone LLM fully frozen, thereby preserving its general capabilities and achieving more faithful generation than competitive baselines. All datasets and code are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/SPARK.

title: Business World Model
ss_tldr: This paper introduces the concept and architecture of a Business World Model (BWM), a world model specialized for business and organizational environments and proposes a business-semantics-centric formulation in which states, dynamics, and feasible actions are linked to business entities, their attributes, and their relationships.
abstract: World model has emerged as a powerful paradigm in artificial intelligence, enabling agents to represent their environments, predict future states, and evaluate possible actions before acting. However, existing world models have largely been developed for visual or physical domains such as computer vision, robotics, gaming, and autonomous driving, which are governed by relatively stable dynamics. These formulations are not directly applicable to business practice, where the relevant environment is semantic, organizational, and market driven. Outcomes depend on context-sensitive factors such as customer behavior, pricing, competition, and regulation. This paper introduces the concept and architecture of a Business World Model, a world model specialized for business and organizational environments. We propose a business-semantics-centric formulation in which states, dynamics, and feasible actions are linked to business entities, their attributes, and their relationships. Within this framework, intelligent agents can simulate alternative action sequences, estimate their effects on future business outcomes, and evaluate trade-offs under uncertainty and business constraints. We present a reference design and open-source implementation in which LLM agents interpret natural-language business goals and explain results, while a deterministic, metadata-driven simulation engine integrating machine learning models, business rules, and action spaces performs all calculations. A churn case study of a digital subscription business demonstrates that the system recommends options meeting the churn-reduction target within the revenue constraint. This work establishes a conceptual foundation for autonomous business systems capable of moving from instruction-based execution toward goal-driven planning, optimization, and execution.

title: NL2AGBench: Benchmarking LLM Auto-Formalization for AlphaGeometry
ss_tldr: The Natural Language to AlphaGeometry Benchmark (NL2AGBench), which evaluates LLMs in translating English geometry problems into AlphaGeometry-compatible formal representations and introduces an error taxonomy distinguishing syntax and logic errors, which yield measurable improvements across multiple model families.
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language understanding and mathematical reasoning. However, their ability to translate informal mathematical problems into formal representations remains underexplored. This limitation is particularly important for neuro-symbolic geometry systems such as AlphaGeometry, whose theorem-proving engine requires inputs in a specialized domain-specific language (DSL). Although AlphaGeometry achieves near-IMO gold-medalist performance, manually converting natural-language problems into its formal syntax remains a significant usability bottleneck. To address this challenge, we introduce the Natural Language to AlphaGeometry Benchmark (NL2AGBench), which evaluates LLMs in translating English geometry problems into AlphaGeometry-compatible formal representations. NL2AGBench uses execution-based verification within AlphaGeometry to assess translation quality rather than relying solely on textual similarity. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art open- and closed-source LLMs across multiple parameter scales and analyze executable translation accuracy, syntactic correctness, and error characteristics. Our experiments reveal a substantial performance gap between closed- and open-source models: leading closed-source models achieve executable translation rates above 80%, while even the largest open-source models struggle to consistently preserve geometric constraints and produce valid formalizations. We introduce an error taxonomy distinguishing syntax and logic errors and investigate mitigation strategies, including few-shot prompting, fine-tuning, and human-guided hinting, which yield measurable improvements across multiple model families.

title: NAS-Driven Hardware Accelerator Exploration for Edge AI and Quantization Effects on the Pareto Space
ss_tldr: A three-stage pipeline is proposed: a hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201, a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control, and an evolutionary Domain Space Exploration backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping.
abstract: Edge AI deployment demands neural architectures that are simultaneously accurate, computationally efficient, and hardware-deployable - a challenge addressed by hardware-aware Neural Architecture Search (NAS). While recent works incorporate quantization directly into the NAS loop, these approaches expand search complexity and tightly couple architecture and quantization design. The simpler post-search quantization strategy has received little analytical attention: the effects of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) on the NAS-discovered Pareto structure remain uncharacterised, and no framework combines quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration. This paper addresses both gaps. First, a three-stage pipeline is proposed: a hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201, a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control, and an evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping. Second, an empirical study characterises how INT4 PTQ perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space through formal stability metrics on ground-truth data for all 15,625 architectures, and demonstrates that an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies.

title: Rational Sparse Autoencoder
ss_tldr: The Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE) is introduced, which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function and strictly improves on it after the fine-tuning step, without sacrificing feature-level interpretability under sparse probing.
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are standard tools for mechanistic interpretability, but current SAE families are constrained by fixed encoder nonlinearities such as ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. This hard-codes a particular sparsity mechanism into the model and can distort the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off. We introduce the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function. The design is motivated by a reconstruction advantage that we prove for RSAE at matched expected sparsity, with guaranteed non-inferiority to ReLU and, under stated assumptions, provable improvements over JumpReLU and TopK. The model is then implemented through a two-stage pipeline: an initialization procedure that copies the pre-trained baseline SAE weights and calibrates the scale parameters along with the rational coefficients; followed by a fine-tuning step under a sparsity-regularized reconstruction objective that holds $\ell_0$ at the teacher's value. Consistent with this theory, on residual-stream activations of three open-weight language models and across all three baseline activation families, the RSAE improves reconstruction fidelity after the fine-tuning step at the same level of sparsity. These gains are consistent across host language models, across baseline activation families, and across the full range of baseline sparsity we tested, while the upgrade itself adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and one training run takes between about 4 and 25 minutes on a single consumer GPU.

title: Mining Architectural Quality Under Agentic AI Adoption: A Causal Study of Java Repositories
ss_tldr: The causal effect of adoption on architectural smell density (ASD) is estimated with a staggered difference-in-differences design and the Borusyak imputation estimator, applying a causal design recently used for code-level metrics to the architecture level.
abstract: AI coding tools are now used by a majority of developers, and agentic use of these tools has popularized the practice colloquially called "vibe coding". Yet causal evidence on their effect on software architecture is scarce. Prior causal work has measured code-level outcomes (complexity, static analysis warnings); whether such degradation propagates to architecture-level outcomes remains unknown. We mine 151 open-source Java repositories, 74 with detectable agentic AI adoption (identified via configuration files and Co-Authored-By commit trailers) and 77 propensity-matched controls, across a 13-month per-repository window yielding 1,811 monthly Arcan snapshots. We estimate the causal effect of adoption on architectural smell density (ASD) with a staggered difference-in-differences design and the Borusyak imputation estimator, applying a causal design recently used for code-level metrics to the architecture level. Total smell counts are essentially unchanged (+1.1%, p = 0.82) while lines of code grow +12.8% (p = 0.003); the resulting 6.7% ASD decline (p = 0.004) is therefore a denominator effect rather than an architectural improvement. Per-type estimates and robustness checks (wild cluster bootstrap, Lee bounds, stale-observation sensitivity) corroborate the pattern; pre-trends are flat (Wald p = 0.90), consistent with parallel trends. Density-normalized outcomes can mislead when treatment affects system size: raw counts and explicit decomposition are required for causal mining studies of AI tool adoption. The complete replication package, including the curated 151-repository monthly panel, is publicly available.

title: Authors' Response to AI-Based Reviews: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
ss_tldr: Findings are reported from two independent pilot studies on authors' use and perceptions of AI-based auxiliary review at two computer science venues about how authors use and perceive AI-based feedback.
abstract: Background: Large language models are increasingly used to assist scholarly peer review, but there is limited evidence about how authors judge their feedback and use it to revise their papers.   Methods: We studied authors' experiences of receiving an auxiliary AI review alongside human reviews in three computer-science cohorts: LifeCLEF 2025, LifeCLEF 2026, and CVWW 2026. Post-review questionnaires yielded 92 responses concerning 71 papers. We summarized closed-ended answers using descriptive statistics and examined free-text responses through thematic analysis.   Results: Most responses rated the AI review useful (82/92 (89%), and 82/92 (89%) reported using at least some of its suggestions in revision. Authors reported that AI identified issues missed by human reviewers ((76/92 (83%). However, 44/92 (48%) trusted AI feedback less than human feedback, and 58/92 (63%) reported incorrect or misleading comments. Authors valued suggestions that improved clarity and reproducibility, but also described overlooked evidence, inappropriate demands, and difficulty finding useful comments within lengthy reviews. They emphasized the need to check AI feedback and retain control over how their manuscripts were processed. Future review by both humans and AI was supported by 85/92 (92%); 83/92 (90%) preferred advance notice and 73/92 (79%) supported explicit consent.   Conclusions: Authors often found AI reviews useful for revision without trusting them as much as human reviews. These exploratory findings favor a supplementary role for AI, with human oversight, clear disclosure, and author consent. They do not establish that AI can replace human reviewers or improve manuscript quality.

title: Towards Embodied Air-Ground Cooperative Object Search: Benchmark, Dataset and Agentic Method
ss_tldr: AGOS-Bench is introduced, the first dedicated benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can integrate aerial discoveries and ground-level verification through UAV-UGV cooperation, and AGOS-Agent is proposed, a training-free and tool-augmented approach to address the AGOS task.
abstract: Air-Ground Object Search (AGOS) in urban environments is a challenging embodied task, which requires an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) and an Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) to jointly search for and verify a specified target vehicle from multi-view visual references. To study this underexplored problem, we introduce AGOS-Bench, the first dedicated benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can integrate aerial discoveries and ground-level verification through UAV-UGV cooperation. We further provide AGOS-Dataset as the companion resource of exemplary trajectories constructed by an automatic pipeline. It consists of 7.7k episodes for searching objects of diverse categories and attributes, spanning three difficulty levels. To address the AGOS task, we propose AGOS-Agent, a training-free and tool-augmented approach. The agentic method relieves VLMs from complex and dynamic coordination via a deliberate search-handoff-verify cooperation protocol, only demanding VLMs for scene understanding and decision-making. Extensive experiments on nine VLMs show that AGOS-Agent improves overall success rate for eight of the nine evaluated backbones while reducing decision steps for all nine. On the hard split, the SR and SPL of Gemini-3.6-Flash increase from 8.6% to 55.7% and from 7.6% to 44.0%, respectively.

title: Zero-Shot Respiratory Sound Classification through LLM-Augmented Audio-Text Alignment
ss_tldr: This work proposes a framework that aligns self-supervised respiratory encoders with medical terminology in a shared latent space turning them into a zero-shot-capable foundation model, and uses a medical LLM to synthesize structured reports from metadata, creating dense semantic anchors for contrastive learning.
abstract: Self-supervised respiratory encoders lack semantic grounding in clinical domain needed for zero-shot inference, limiting their utility without task-specific labeled data. We propose a framework that aligns these encoders with medical terminology in a shared latent space turning them into a zero-shot-capable foundation model. To address paired data scarcity, we use a medical LLM to synthesize structured reports from metadata, creating dense semantic anchors for contrastive learning. Our training combines a sigmoid-based contrastive loss with encoder's native SSL objective and similarity-aware negative sampling to sharpen pathological boundaries. Across 9 tasks on 6 datasets, our method achieves a 61.3% mean zero-shot AUC, surpassing CLAP (51.4%) and Qwen2-Audio (54.9%) while reaching the highest linear probing AUC (71.6%) with only 43% of data used by full-scale baselines, showing that structured semantic alignment outperforms large-scale, general-purpose models in clinical diagnostics.

title: Learning Which Evidence-Seeking Decisions Matter: Calibrated Counterfactual Replay for Language Agents
ss_tldr: Carefully scoped counterfactual credit, paired with validity gating, diagnostics, and verifiable constraints, provides a reproducible route toward more reliable long-horizon RL for language agents.
abstract: Language agents answer questions by searching, reading, and checking claims. A reward on the final answer says little about which of those decisions earned it, since an agent can reach the right string after redundant searches or with half the evidence missing. We treat the question as an experiment. At a saved decision point, PCCC-RL, for prefix-conditioned counterfactual credit, restores the tool state, runs the action the agent chose alongside a feasible alternative, and lets the same frozen policy finish both branches. The difference in final score then samples what the decision was worth. Replaying everything is too expensive, so the method predicts each action's credit up front, checks a random subset, and uses the recorded selection probabilities to correct the errors of that prediction, spending the budget where a further check can still move the training signal. Alternatives are drawn from the prefix alone, which keeps the comparison a usable gradient baseline. On HotpotQA and MuSiQue, joint exact match, requiring a correct answer together with complete supporting evidence, reaches 56.71% and 36.82%, gains of 4.19 and 3.86 points over a baseline with the same replay access. The gain concentrates in complete evidence chains and accumulates over many updates. Single-update effects stay uncertain, and citation coverage and scope distinctions such as "none" versus "not all" remain open.

title: Channel-wise Vector Quantization: Native 1D Visual Tokenization with Learnable Ordering
ss_tldr: This work presents Channel-wise Vector Quantization (CVQ), a novel image tokenization paradigm that replaces patch-wise tokens with channel-wise tokens, and introduces a new visual autoregressive framework with "next-channel prediction".
abstract: We present Channel-wise Vector Quantization (CVQ), a novel image tokenization paradigm that replaces patch-wise tokens with channel-wise tokens. Unlike conventional vector quantization, which assigns a discrete token to each patch feature vector, CVQ quantizes each channel of the feature map. This represents an image as a 1D channel sequence with learnable coarse-to-fine ordering, rather than a 2D patch grid. Based on CVQ, we introduce a new visual autoregressive framework with "next-channel prediction". Instead of rendering images patch by patch in raster order, our Channel-wise Autoregressive (CAR) model predicts image channels sequentially, producing progressively enriched visual details. Specifically, it first sketches global structure and then refines fine-grained attributes, akin to a human artist's workflow. Empirically, we show that: (1) CVQ exhibits strong codebook scalability, maintaining 95%+ utilization with up to $2^{16}$ entries while delivering growing reconstruction gains over VQ as the codebook scales up; and (2) CAR attains a DPG score of 86.7 and a GenEval score of 0.79, demonstrating strong effectiveness for text-to-image generation.

title: EvoSkill Injection: Red-Teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in Self-Evolving Agents
ss_tldr: A red-teaming framework for evaluating this threat model targeting the autonomous skill generation and evolution pipeline of self-evolving agents and shows that SARGE induces malicious skill formation and that injected skills are persistently stored and repeatedly activated, highlighting the risk of persistent capability corruption.
abstract: LLM-based agent systems increasingly adopt skill-based architectures to reduce repetitive reasoning costs and improve stable, efficient task execution. Recent studies propose self-evolving agents that autonomously generate, refine, and reuse skills from past experiences to enable continuous capability evolution. However, autonomous skill evolution introduces a new attack surface in which malicious capabilities are generated, stored, and reused as legitimate skills. In this paper, we define EvoSkill Injection as a threat model targeting the autonomous skill generation and evolution pipeline of self-evolving agents. We further propose SARGE (Red-teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in self-evolving agents), a red-teaming framework for evaluating this threat model through iterative generation, escalation, and reinforcement interactions. To support our framework, we construct EvoSkillBench, a benchmark dataset of malicious interaction trajectories for inducing malicious skill formation in self-evolving agents, and introduce EvoSkillSafetyBench, a post-attack benchmark for evaluating whether injected malicious skills are subsequently retrieved and activated as harmful behaviors. Our evaluation shows that SARGE induces malicious skill formation and that injected skills are persistently stored and repeatedly activated, highlighting the risk of persistent capability corruption.

title: Random coloured digraphs defined by a Markov logic network
ss_tldr: It is shown that, for every choice of weights, if the weights are scaled by $1/n$ then, for every first-order sentence $\varphi$ the probability that $\varphi$ holds tends to either 0 or 1 as $n \to \infty$; that is, a 0-1 law for first-order logic holds.
abstract: A Markov Logic Network (MLN) $M$ is a probabilistic relational model used in Statistical Relational Artificial Intelligence for defining a probability distribution $P_D^M$ on the set $W_D$ of possible worlds with domain $D$ for an arbitrary finite domain $D$. An MLN consists of first-order formulas, which we call soft constraints, with associated weights which are nonnegative real numbers. The behaviour of the probability distribution, including the effect of the weights, on different domain sizes is poorly understood. We approach the problem in a systematic way by studying sequences $(P_n^M(ψ) : n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)$ where $ψ$ is a first-order sentence and $P_n^M(ψ)$ is the probability that $ψ$ holds in $W_D$ where $D = [n] := \{1, \ldots, n\}$. We consider a first-order language that can express a property $P(x)$ and relation $R(x, y)$ and show that all of the following cases can be realized for an MLN $M$ such that each of its soft constraints is a boolean combination of $P(x)$, $P(y)$ and $R(x, y)$ in which both $x$ and $y$ appears:  For every first-order sentence $ψ$, $P_n^M(ψ)$ converges to 0 or 1 as $n\to\infty$. For every first-order sentence $ψ$, $P_n^M(ψ)$ converges as $n\to\infty$ but not necessarily to 0 or 1. There is a first-order sentence $ψ$ such that $P_n^M(ψ)$ does not converge as $n\to\infty$. In fact, all three cases can be realized even after fixing the soft constraints and, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, by varying their weights by less than $\varepsilon$. We also show that, given any MLN as described above, we can efficiently determine which case it belongs to by inspecting the MLN. Then we show that if the weights are scaled by $1/n$ then we end up in case~(1) no matter how the weights are chosen.

title: VideoEditor-MoE: Scaling Complex Video Editing with Mixture of Experts
ss_tldr: VideoEditor-MoE is introduced, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing that identifies decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling and expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens.
abstract: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.

title: Releasing the Inner Jev: A Simple Recipe for Open Decision Models
ss_tldr: It is shown that existing open instruction-tuned language models can achieve comparable performance with Jev by reading out answers from letters in the model's output logits at the last token position, and with simple fine-tuning they outperform Jev on a wide range of decision tasks.
abstract: LLM-based decision-making systems, also called System One models, have recently gained popularity, most notably through Jev (Almeida, 2026). Given a typed input state, a question, and a set of options, they return a calibrated probability for each option in a single forward pass, without text generation. We show that open instruction-tuned LLMs can achieve performance comparable to Jev without any additional training, by reading out answers from letters (A, B, C, etc.) in the model's output logits at the last token position. Next, we propose a simple supervised LoRA fine-tuning recipe that can improve their performance further. We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs: Gemma 4 31B, Gemma 4 12B, Qwen3.6-27B, and Qwen3.5-4B. Furthermore, we introduce OpenDecisions, a novel 2,352-question validation dataset designed to reflect the task composition of JevBench (JevBench maintainers, 2026) and which computes a Capability score based on accuracy and calibration. Without fine-tuning, Gemma 4 31B scores 79.6 on OpenDecisions, compared to Jev's 80.1. After fine-tuning, it scores 89.0, outperforming Jev by 8.9 Capability points and on par with the strongest open decision model we evaluated. The same recipe improves the three other models by 7.8 to 15.7 points. On a suite of public decision datasets, our models achieve accuracy and calibration comparable to Jev. Our results show that open LLMs already possess System One capabilities, and with simple fine-tuning they outperform Jev on a wide range of decision tasks. We release our models, training and serving code, OpenDecisions, and DecisionBank, our training dataset consisting of 261,561 decisions.

title: Can Computation from Earlier Problems Help LLMs Solve New Ones?
ss_tldr: To improve reasoning under retained history, STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse) is introduced, which improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history.
abstract: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? Preliminary experiments show that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To trace this effect, we hold each problem fixed and vary its preceding history. The resulting changes in the model's internal states contain a recurring, problem-dependent component. To improve reasoning with retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). It captures attention keys and values from earlier response generation in a read-only bank. STAIR learns to reflect current query vectors to redirect attention over this bank during prompt processing. The backbone and stored entries remain fixed; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four reasoning benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history. The math-trained Qwen3.5-9B controller also improves code generation on HumanEval+ without further training.

title: UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval
ss_tldr: This work introduces \textsc{UpliftMem}, which learns memory retrieval from set-level execution uplift relative to the same executor without memory, and achieves the best success rates among evaluated baselines on the main evaluation sets.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents draw on external memory to guide new tasks, raising the question of which memories to retrieve together to improve execution. Learning set values requires outcome feedback, but evaluating each untested alternative costs an additional rollout. We introduce \textsc{UpliftMem}, which learns set-level execution uplift relative to the same executor without memory. Our analysis of how retrieval preferences limit feedback coverage motivates targeted probes. Under a correlated Gaussian surrogate, we derive a closed-form expected value of sample information (EVSI) criterion that prioritizes probes by their expected benefit to local retrieval decisions. The feedback trains a shared scorer with the executor frozen, and inference requires no probing. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and BigCodeBench, \textsc{UpliftMem} achieves best or joint-best success rates among evaluated methods. On fixed-store MemSyco-Bench evaluations, decision accuracy increases from 41.7\% to 66.5\% with Qwen3-4B and from 44.4\% to 68.8\% with Qwen3-8B. At matched probe budgets, EVSI improves decision accuracy over random probing by 10.6 and 13.9 percentage points, respectively.

title: How to "train" a surgeon? Benchmarking generalist agents in surgical scene understanding
ss_tldr: SurgAgentGym is introduced, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks and shows that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks.
abstract: Evaluating general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for surgical scene understanding remains limited due to scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols. We address these challenges through a two-stage evaluation framework for surgical scene understanding. In Stage I, we introduce SurgKnowBench, a diagnostic benchmark that harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks and evaluates proprietary and open-source MLLMs to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgKnowBench reveals that current models retain partial visual priors but remain weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Building on this failure frontier and motivated by the scaffolded nature of surgical training, we introduce SurgAgentGym, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks. SurgAgentGym evaluates whether generalist agents can improve surgical understanding at inference time through tool-mediated evidence use, without additional surgical training. Our results show that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. This opens a path toward future studies of agentic surgical understanding.

title: DeepEdu-F: A Framework for Efficient and Scalable Agentic LLMs in Vietnamese Education
ss_tldr: DeepEdu-v1, an AI-tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE (Self-improving Context-Aware Learning Engine), a framework with two innovations intended to progressively reduce reliance on dominant-language priors as trustworthy local knowledge accumulates is presented.
abstract: Cloud AI assistants send student data to foreign servers, conflicting with data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53, and are not grounded in the national curriculum, so they often hallucinate on local content. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but faces two costs that weight quantization does not remove. An AI tutoring session revisits the same long material every turn, so once prefix caching removes the prefill cost, decoding over a growing KV Cache dominates response time; and grounding the tutor in local knowledge by fine-tuning is too costly to repeat as that knowledge changes. We present DeepEdu-F, a framework for the Vietnamese AI tutor DeepEdu with two components. LastSet selects the critical KV Cache entries once per turn from the question's attention, decodes the whole turn from that set, and keeps the full cache so later questions can select again. REPAIR (Reliable Evidence-based Playbook Adaptation and Insight Revision) curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of updating weights. LastSet decodes up to 3.1x faster than dense decoding at a 256k-token context, faster than four sparse baselines, with accuracy close to full attention. Compared with ACE (ADD), REPAIR raises final accuracy from 70.0% to 80.5% on Formula and from 53.6% to 59.7% on FiNER, while mean task/scenario goal completion across AppWorld's normal and challenge splits increases from 9.28% to 16.28%.

title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
ss_tldr: Whether agent code survives longer than human code is decided as much by the measurement as by the code, and an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies is derived.
abstract: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce. Within repositories, no specification detects a difference. LLM intent classifiers agree with human labels about as well as two humans agree with each other, whereas keyword rules do not (kappa = 0.69 to 0.72 against 0.38), and the two reach different verdicts on why agent code is modified. Humans make most modifications to agent code under every unit and window. Re-run on our data, five published designs each change their result with a single choice. Whether agent code survives longer than human code is therefore decided as much by the measurement as by the code. We derive an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies.

title: What the Trace Shows and What the Label Says: Auditing Behavioral Detectors in Agent Evaluation
ss_tldr: These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should come with the trace evidence behind it, whether the question the detector asks applied to that trace, whether the run was cut off by an execution limit, and any human corrections.
abstract: LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, yet evaluations rarely report whether a measurement actually fits the trace it describes. We study what happens when those measurements do not fully capture the trace's behavior. Agents solve GSM8K problems with a calculator whose outputs are occasionally corrupted, which gives ground truth for what the tool returned, what the model later used, and what the detectors reported; a chemistry task with search and retrieval tests the case where the model cannot recompute the tool's output. Across eight models and up to 1,000 traces per model, final correctness, visible re-verification, and fault propagation disagree in systematic ways. The most common gap is the silent tool-output override: the model replaces a corrupted value without calling the tool again, so the error stops propagating while a verification detector records no re-check. Human review finds verification labels the least reliable (\k{appa} =0.29), and checking depends on the task: the same calculator that several models re-checked on arithmetic was never re-checked on chemistry. Execution limits and serving failures also change what is measured. These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should be reported with its evidence, whether the detector's question applied, whether the run was censored, and any human corrections. Our trace viewer makes this information inspectable alongside the reported results.

title: Safeguarding LLMs via Model-Agnostic Latent Safety Signals from Dark Knowledge
ss_tldr: This work introduces LADE (Latent Safety Signals for Defense), which leverages latent safety signals extracted by contrasting harmful and benign queries from dark knowledge in the first-token output probability distribution, and shows that these signals consistently align across LLMs, forming a model-agnostic direction that emerges from safety alignment.
abstract: LLMs have advanced rapidly, raising growing concerns about their safety. Recent work has proposed approaches to detect and defend against attacks including defenses at decoding stage that leverage models' hidden states. However, existing decoding-stage defenses suffer from two limitations. First, they introduce a trade-off between safety and over-refusal, where strengthening safety degrades the model's helpfulness on benign queries. Second, many of these methods rely on internal hidden states and are thus restricted to specific architectures, incurring substantial overhead and limited generalization across models. To address these limitations, we introduce LADE (Latent Safety Signals for Defense), which leverages latent safety signals extracted by contrasting harmful and benign queries from dark knowledge (i.e., information carried by the output probability distribution beyond its argmax) in the first-token output probability distribution. Our key insight is that, beyond surface-level refusal tokens, the dark knowledge in the first-token distribution contains latent safety signals, defined as tokens whose probabilities differ sharply between harmful and benign queries. We show that these signals consistently align across LLMs, forming a model-agnostic direction that emerges from safety alignment. LADE consists of three components: (1) Extracting Latent Safety Signals from Dark Knowledge, which selects top-k safety-discriminative tokens from the first-token probability distribution; (2) Tokenizer Mapping, which maps these tokens across different tokenizers to enable model-agnostic application; and (3) kNN-based Discrimination, which classifies queries via a k-Nearest Neighbors search over the mapped tokens. Across diverse LLMs and benchmarks, LADE is robust against a wide range of jailbreak attacks and lowers attack success rates while maintaining a competitive safety-utility trade-off.

title: Controllable Chains of Thought Can Reveal Less, Even Without Evasion Training
ss_tldr: It is discovered that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model, and these model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations.
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
ss_tldr: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies, is proposed.
abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

title: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling
ss_tldr: 2D Gum-Net is presented, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised and improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged, suggesting that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.
abstract: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $Φ$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.

title: Best-of-Depth: Learning Exploratory Dynamics in Looped Transformers
